title: Why a booster jab works: the second immune response
examples: Why do we need booster vaccines?
Why do you only get chickenpox once?

figure.name: x-compare
figure.verdict: A vaccine is a safe first meeting

explain.say: Most people only catch chickenpox once in their life. Why not twice? Your immune system has a memory! Let's compare the first time it meets a germ with the second time.

draw.text: Why a booster jab works: the second immune response

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: A vaccine is a safe first meeting

explain.say: Look at the left side, the first meeting. Your white blood cells have never seen this germ. Finding the right ones and making antibodies, proteins that stick to germs, takes a week or two. Meanwhile, what might happen to you?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: A vaccine is a safe first meeting

explain.say: Now the right side. After that first fight, your body keeps memory cells, white blood cells that remember the germ's shape. The next time, they spring into action within days. Which side is faster?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: A vaccine is a safe first meeting

explain.say: See the third line on each side? The second time, many more antibodies are made, so the germ is wiped out before you even feel ill. That is what being immune means. Can you explain it back to me?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: A vaccine is a safe first meeting

explain.say: A vaccine gives your body a safe first meeting, using a harmless part of the germ, and a booster makes the memory stronger. Well done! Wow fact: some memory cells can last for decades.

draw.verdict: A vaccine is a safe first meeting

faq.q: What happens the first time I meet a germ?
faq.a: This is the primary response. It takes time for the right white blood cells, called lymphocytes, to be found and multiply and start making antibodies, so you may become ill while they catch up.
asks: Tell me about the first meeting

faq.a: Memory cells are long-lived lymphocytes made after an infection or vaccine. They recognise the same pathogen again and quickly start producing lots of antibodies.
asks: Tell me about the second meeting

faq.a: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by lymphocytes. Each one fits a particular antigen on a pathogen, sticking germs together and marking them to be destroyed.
A vaccine contains a dead or weakened pathogen, a harmless piece of it, or instructions to make a piece. The body responds as if infected and makes memory cells, without becoming ill.

faq.q: Why do we need booster vaccines?
faq.a: A booster is a later dose of a vaccine. It triggers the faster, stronger secondary response, making more memory cells, so protection lasts longer.
asks: Why do some vaccines need a second dose?

facts: In the secondary immune response, antibodies are made faster and in much larger amounts than in the primary response.
Memory lymphocytes can persist for many years, giving long-lasting immunity.
